source: College Board, Assessment Framework for the Digital SAT Suite, Reading and Writing section (content domains, skill/knowledge testing points, and question distribution). Testing points are written from the framework's skill descriptions; check the wording against the PDF before quoting it.

notes: Every question is four-option multiple choice with one best answer; there are no typed answers in Reading and Writing.
Each question has its own short passage (or a pair of passages for Cross-text connections). Literature passages can be prose, poetry or drama, including texts written before 1900.
Within each module, questions are grouped by domain and, within a skill, ordered from easier to harder.
Some Information and Ideas questions pair the passage with a table or graph (Command of evidence: quantitative).

skills.name: Words in context
skills.summary: Students determine the meaning of a high-utility academic word or phrase in context, or choose the most logical and precise word or phrase for a context.
testingPoints: Determine the meaning of a high-utility academic word or phrase as it is used in a text.
Determine which word or phrase most logically and precisely completes a text, given its context.
Use the surrounding sentences, not the word's most common meaning, to decide what the word must mean here.
Distinguish a word's precise meaning in context from near-synonyms that don't fit the text's tone, logic or level of certainty.

skills.name: Text structure and purpose
skills.summary: Students analyze the structure of a text or determine its main rhetorical purpose, or the function of a part of the text.
testingPoints: Determine the main purpose of a text.
Describe the overall structure of a text (for example, a claim followed by a counterexample, or a problem followed by a proposed solution).
Determine the function of a sentence or portion of a text in relation to the text as a whole.
Describe the purpose or structure of a literary text, including poetry and drama.

skills.name: Cross-text connections
skills.summary: Students draw reasonable connections between two topically related texts, such as how the author of one text would respond to the other.
testingPoints: Identify how the author of one text would most likely respond to a claim, finding or method described in the other text.
Determine how two texts relate: whether they agree, disagree, or one qualifies, extends or offers a different explanation for the other.
Identify the specific point on which two texts differ or agree.
Keep each author's view separate from views the author only reports.

skills.name: Central ideas and details
skills.summary: Students determine the central idea of a text and/or interpret its key details.
testingPoints: Determine the central idea or main point of a text.
Identify a key detail that the text states directly.
Interpret how a detail supports or develops the central idea.
Determine the central idea of a literary text, including what a character or speaker thinks, feels or wants.

skills.name: Command of evidence: textual
skills.summary: Students determine which textual evidence best supports, illustrates or challenges a specified claim or point.
testingPoints: Identify the finding or statement that would most directly support a claim or hypothesis made in the text.
Identify the finding or statement that would most directly weaken or challenge a claim or hypothesis.
Identify the quotation from a literary work (often a poem) that best illustrates a claim about it.
Distinguish evidence that addresses the exact claim from evidence that is only on the same topic.

skills.name: Command of evidence: quantitative
skills.summary: Students use data from an informational graphic (a table, bar graph or line graph) to support, illustrate or challenge a claim, or to complete an example.
testingPoints: Use data from a table or graph to complete a statement so that it accurately illustrates a claim in the text.
Identify which data from a table or graph best support or weaken a claim.
Read the graphic's labels, units and categories precisely, and use only the data the claim is about.
Reject choices that are accurate readings of the graphic but don't address the claim.

skills.name: Inferences
skills.summary: Students draw reasonable inferences based on explicit and implicit information and ideas in a text, typically by choosing the choice that most logically completes the text.
testingPoints: Determine the conclusion that most logically follows from the information in a text.
Combine two or more pieces of information in a text to reach a conclusion it doesn't state outright.
Recognize what a finding does and doesn't allow a researcher to conclude.
Reject conclusions that go beyond what the text supports, even when they sound plausible.

skills.name: Boundaries
skills.summary: Students edit text to conform to the conventions of Standard English sentence structure and punctuation.
testingPoints: Punctuate the boundary between two independent clauses (period, semicolon, colon, or comma with a coordinating conjunction); avoid comma splices, run-ons and fragments.
Punctuate supplementary elements within a sentence (nonessential clauses, appositives, parenthetical phrases) with matching commas, dashes or parentheses.
Use colons and dashes to introduce explanations, lists and elaborations.
Punctuate items in a series, including series that need semicolons.
Avoid unnecessary punctuation, such as a comma between a subject and its verb or between a verb and its object.
Punctuate a sentence that ends with a question or contains a quotation.

skills.name: Form, structure, and sense
skills.summary: Students edit text to conform to the conventions of Standard English usage.
testingPoints: Make a verb agree with its subject, including when other words come between them or the subject follows the verb.
Make a pronoun agree with its antecedent in number, and choose the correct pronoun case.
Use the verb tense, aspect and mood that fit the sentence and the surrounding text.
Use the correct form of plural and possessive nouns and determiners (for example, its/it's, their/they're).
Place a modifier so that it clearly modifies the right word (avoid dangling and misplaced modifiers).
Use finite and nonfinite verb forms (infinitives, participles, gerunds) correctly within a sentence.

skills.name: Rhetorical synthesis
skills.summary: Students strategically integrate information and ideas on a topic, given as bulleted notes, to accomplish a specified rhetorical goal.
testingPoints: Choose the sentence that uses the relevant notes to accomplish a stated goal (for example, emphasize a difference, introduce a study to an unfamiliar audience, or present a finding).
Match the goal precisely: a choice must do what the question asks, not just restate accurate notes.
Use only information that appears in the notes.

skills.name: Transitions
skills.summary: Students determine the most effective transition word or phrase to logically connect information and ideas in a text.
testingPoints: Determine the logical relationship between two sentences or ideas: addition, contrast, cause and effect, example, sequence, concession or emphasis.
Choose the transition word or phrase that signals that relationship.
Read the sentence before and the sentence after the blank, not just the sentence with the blank.
